text: A contract summarizer scores well on ROUGE against reference summaries. After launch, legal reviewers find summaries that cite clause numbers that do not exist in the source. What is the main gap in the evaluation?
options: The reference summary set was too small to compute ROUGE reliably
The evaluation did not track latency alongside summary quality
The evaluation should have used a larger model to write the references
It measured word overlap only, with no check of claims against the source
correct_answer: It measured word overlap only, with no check of claims against the source
explanation: ROUGE measures word overlap with a reference, not whether claims are true to the source document. The missing piece is a faithfulness check (D), such as verifying each cited clause against the source with a code check or a calibrated judge. A bigger reference set (A) or better references (C) would still measure overlap only. Latency (B) is a separate dimension that does not explain invented clauses.

text: Right after a weekly document refresh, a RAG assistant starts giving confident but wrong answers. The model version, prompt, and latency are unchanged. What should you check first?
options: Whether the system prompt needs stronger instructions about accuracy
Whether the correct chunk appears in the top-K for the failing questions
Whether a larger model tier would answer the failing questions correctly instead
Whether the model's effort setting was lowered during the refresh
correct_answer: Whether the correct chunk appears in the top-K for the failing questions
explanation: Correlate the symptom with what changed: the only change was the data, so check retrieval and indexing first (B). A broken re-index or stale chunks feed bad context, and the model answers faithfully from it. The prompt (A), model tier (C), and effort (D) did not change, so they cannot explain a regression that began with the refresh.

text: An LLM judge compares two answers side by side and picks the better one. The team notices it picks the first answer far more often than chance. What is the standard mitigation?
options: Run each comparison in both orders and count only consistent wins
Switch the judge to a 1-to-10 quality scale instead of pairwise choice
Ask the judge to give its score first and its reasoning afterward
Use the same model and prompt as the system being evaluated
correct_answer: Run each comparison in both orders and count only consistent wins
explanation: This is position bias. Running each pair in both orders and counting only consistent wins (A) cancels it. A vague 1-to-10 scale (B) produces noisier, drifting scores. The judge should reason before scoring, not after (C). Using the same model as the system under test (D) adds self-preference bias instead of removing bias.

text: A team tunes its prompt for weeks against the same 200 test cases until it scores 96%. In production, quality is clearly lower. Which dataset practice did they skip?
options: Writing every test case by hand instead of using production samples
Generating thousands of synthetic cases without expert review
Keeping a held-out test set that is scored but never tuned against
Removing hard and ambiguous cases so scores are more stable
correct_answer: Keeping a held-out test set that is scored but never tuned against
explanation: Iterate on a development set and keep a held-out test set that is scored but never tuned against (C). Tuning on the test set produces scores that do not survive production. Good sets start from real production traffic, not only hand-written cases (A). Synthetic cases need expert review before they count (B). Hard and ambiguous cases should be included on purpose (D), not removed.

text: An assistant's answers suddenly became longer and it calls tools more often. Nobody changed the prompt, the data, or the code. The application calls the model through an alias rather than a pinned ID. What should you check first?
options: Whether the retrieval index was rebuilt with a different embedding model
Whether the prompt has emphatic rules that confuse the model
Whether user questions have become harder over the same period
Which model ID actually served the requests before and after the change
correct_answer: Which model ID actually served the requests before and after the change
explanation: Behavior that changes with no prompt or data change points to the model itself, here most likely an alias that now resolves to a newer model. Check which model ID served the requests (D), then pin the ID and evaluate old and new side by side. The index (A) and prompt (B) did not change. Harder questions (C) would not explain a sudden shift in tool use and length.
